16.0.0.en: Ziba: the servant of Mephibosheth (ch. 9). Bottle: a skin vessel for keeping liquids.

16.0.1.en: Ziba came to David while he was on the Mount of Olives and presented him with a gift consisting of two donkeys, two hundred loaves of bread, bunches of grapes, a hundred cakes of figs, and a skin of wine. Ziba did this expecting David to triumph over Absalom's rebellion, so that good would come to him from David.

16.1.1.en: David asked him why he had brought all this, and Ziba answered that the donkeys were for the king's household to ride on, to ease the weariness of the journey, the bread and figs for the king's soldiers to eat, and the wine for those who might grow weary from walking in the wilderness, since wine was used at that time as a remedy for some illnesses.

16.2.0.en: David asked Ziba about Mephibosheth the son of Saul, and he answered him that he was in Jerusalem. Here Ziba seized the opportunity to slander Mephibosheth falsely, claiming that he was pleased with the events taking place, in the hope that the present conflict between David and Absalom would end in his favor, that is, in Mephibosheth's favor, and the people would choose Mephibosheth as king over them. The truth is that Mephibosheth was innocent of this charge and wished to come to meet David as he left Jerusalem, but Ziba deceived him and went without him (ch. 19:26).

16.3.0.en: The king believed Ziba's words and was angry with Mephibosheth, whom he had honored and treated well: how could he repay kindness with evil? Therefore he issued a decree that everything he had given to Mephibosheth of possessions and lands should be given to his servant Ziba. Ziba rejoiced and bowed down in thanks to the king, and prayed for him, wishing that the king's favor toward him and care for him might continue.

16.3.1.en: David benefited from Ziba's conduct toward him in the following ways:

16.3.2.en: 1 - Discipline from God: as one of his commanders, Uriah, was betrayed by David, so now Mephibosheth, to whom David had done much good, betrays him.

16.3.3.en: 2 -David and his men needed the food that Ziba brought.

16.3.4.en: 3 -David learned not to be hasty in his judgments on Mephibosheth, for he understood afterward that he had been wronged and that Ziba was the traitor.

16.3.5.en: Do not betray those around you and deal treacherously with them to gain quick profits, for God sees you, and you will lose later on earth and then lose your place in the Kingdom.

16.4.s.en: (2) Shimei son of Gera curses David

16.4.0.en: Bahurim: a village near the Mount of Olives, lying between it and the Jordan River; its site is now "Ras et-Tamim."

16.4.1.en: David and his men reached the village of Bahurim, and behold, a man came out from it to meet them, Shimei son of Gera, one of the inhabitants of that village, who belonged to the tribe of Benjamin and the clan of Saul. He was gloating over what had befallen David, so he began to curse him with harsh words and to throw stones at him, he and his men, as a sign of insult and spite. Of course the stones and dust did not reach David and his men, but they were signs of hatred and gloating, because Shimei was walking on one hill and David and his men on another, with a valley separating them.

16.5.0.en: Bloody man: a man of wars and bloodshed.

16.5.1.en: Man of Belial: a wicked man, because he is attributed to Belial, who is a pagan god.

16.5.2.en: The LORD hath returned upon thee all the blood of the house of Saul: the Lord has taken vengeance on you for those of the house of Saul who died.

16.5.3.en: What this man said was a plain expression of his gloating over David, asking him never to return to Jerusalem, which he had left, and accusing him of being a man thirsty for bloodshed. He supposed that King David was the cause of the death of Abner son of Ner and of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and therefore that he was a wicked man who had seized the kingdom from the house of Saul, and now the Lord was taking vengeance on him for those evils, taking the kingdom from him and giving it to his son Absalom, and that the misfortunes that had befallen him were nothing but a sign of the Lord's vengeance on him and on his deeds. Yet this was the opposite of the truth, for David had not killed anyone of the house of Saul, and he had fought the wars of the Lord to triumph over the pagans.

16.6.0.en: Sons of Zeruiah: Zeruiah was David's sister and the mother of Joab and his two brothers Abishai and Asahel.

16.6.1.en: Abishai, one of David's chief commanders, was enraged by this man's behavior and described him as a mere contemptible dog of no worth, and asked the king's permission to go over to him and cut off his head. The king rebuked him and made him understand that his opinion did not agree with what the king himself saw, and that he should not work to silence Shimei, for he was only an instrument the Lord used to discipline David, because God was displeased with him on account of his sin. David was not willing then to punish Shimei, just as Christ was not willing for Peter to use his sword in defending Christ when He was arrested.

16.6.2.en: Do not be vexed with those who wrong you, but accept this from the hand of God and examine yourself, perhaps you are at fault in something toward God. Make excuses for those who wrong you and forgive them.

16.7.0.en: David wanted to lessen the impact of Shimei's insolence on his men, so he urged them not to be surprised at his conduct: if his own son, David's son who came from his own loins, was pursuing him, it was no wonder that a man of the tribe of Benjamin and of the clan of Saul should do what he was doing in cursing and insulting him. He repeated his request to them to let the man say what he pleased, for he deserved that insult, since the Lord was the one who had allowed it.

16.8.0.en: David hopes that God will reward him for accepting the insult, considering that it came by God's permission, and will give him mercy by forgiving his sins.

16.9.0.en: Shimei continued to curse David and to throw dust and stones at him and his men, expressing his contempt and gloating.

16.10.0.en: Because of the length of the journey and the intense grief of all the people, weariness overcame them, so they turned aside to a place in the wilderness of the Jordan to rest from the toil of the journey.

16.11.s.en: (3) Hushai as a counselor to Absalom

16.11.0.en: On the other side, Absalom's advance and the men who had joined him reached Jerusalem, together with Ahithophel his counselor, and the time of his arrival coincided with the arrival of Hushai the Archite, to carry out what David had instructed him. As soon as he arrived in Jerusalem, Hushai the Archite began to draw close to Absalom, declaring his complete loyalty to him and proclaiming him king.

16.12.0.en: Absalom found it strange that Hushai had left David in his crisis as he fled from Jerusalem, and he asked him the reason for his lack of loyalty to him.

16.13.0.en: Hushai denied having betrayed David, and wisely claimed that he would serve the one whom the Lord and the people had chosen as king over them, especially since he was the son of his lord David and not a stranger to him, and he added that he was ready to be as loyal to him as he had been loyal to David. Hushai meant David, because he was the one whom God had chosen, but Absalom, in his pride, supposed that he was the one chosen by God.

16.13.1.en: If your intention is good, God will help you and give you favor in the eyes of others, and will use you in every good work and give you wisdom in every action.

16.14.s.en: (4) Absalom goes in to his father's concubines

16.14.0.en: As soon as Absalom entered Jerusalem, he asked Ahithophel, who was considered the most important of the king's counselors, together with those with him, what he should do at the beginning of his reign.

16.15.0.en: Ahithophel advised Absalom to lie with the ten concubines who had stayed behind and not fled with David, and had remained in Jerusalem to look after David's house. Then the people would hear and be certain that this conduct of Absalom's would anger David and would leave no room for the possibility of reconciliation between Absalom and his father, and they would work with all their might to establish Absalom as king, for otherwise, if David got hold of them, he would strike them down with a terrible blow. So there would be no going back from the rebellion they had carried out.

16.16.0.en: Absalom carried out Ahithophel's advice, and they pitched a tent for him on the roof of the royal palace so that he might lie in it with David's women in the sight of all Israel, so that the people would know that the relations between him and his father had become completely strained, with no going back.

16.16.1.en: We recall here that it was from this roof that David cast an evil look at Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite and then fell with her, and now God allows him to be disciplined by his son's adultery with his concubines.

16.17.0.en: It was known to all that Ahithophel was a wise and experienced man whose counsel never failed, and both David and Absalom valued his counsel very highly and regarded what he said as though it were from God. Ahithophel wanted to show Absalom's enmity toward his father, and then to have David killed by the hand of Absalom and his men, because he feared that David would be reconciled with Absalom, forgive him and return to his kingdom, and then take vengeance on Ahithophel himself, the author of the evil counsels.

16.17.1.en: Intelligence and wisdom are great gifts that divine providence grants in varying degrees, so let us use them for good and not for evil, lest we fall under judgment "when we are asked to give an account of our stewardship."

17.0.0.en: After Ahithophel gave his first counsel concerning David's concubines, and Absalom carried it out, he now gives him the second counsel, concerning the war plan he advises him to follow, which was as follows: Ahithophel would choose 12,000 warriors to be under his command and would surprise David that very night. The shock of the surprise would confuse David and his men, especially as they were weary from the long journey, so the king would be alarmed and unable to lead his men, and they would flee, and then it would be easy to strike the king and kill him.

17.0.1.en: Ahithophel's counsel shows the extent of his betrayal of David, who had cared for him and looked after him for many years, for he resembles Judas Iscariot. To carry the betrayal further, he wanted to lead the army, perhaps so that he might have a greater position in the new kingdom.

17.1.0.en: By the killing of David, all the people who were with him would return to Absalom and no one else would be killed, and peace would prevail. David here partly signifies Christ, of whom Caiaphas the high priest prophesied that He must die for the Jewish nation so that it might obtain salvation, and this was a prophecy from God on the mouth of Caiaphas (Jn 11:49, 50). Here Ahithophel says that by the killing of David the people would obtain peace and the ranks would unite behind Absalom, but God did not allow the death of David here, and Ahithophel's plan and counsel were rejected, as we shall see in the following verses.

17.2.0.en: Absalom and all his men were persuaded by Ahithophel's counsel. In truth it was a very sound plan in every respect, for surprise always has a great effect in military tactics; and ending the fighting without bloodshed would please the people and raise Absalom in their eyes, since he did not wish to harm any of them.

17.2.1.en: May you appreciate the kindness and favor of anyone who has helped you in anything in your life, not only by giving thanks to God, but also by doing a service for him or for those around him as far as you can. But at the very least, do nothing against him, lest you be a traitor to him like Judas Iscariot.

17.3.s.en: (2) The counsel of Hushai the Archite

17.3.0.en: Absalom asked for Hushai the Archite to be summoned, so that he might benefit from his experience as well and learn from him whether he supported the opinion of the other counselor, Ahithophel, so that all would agree on one opinion, or whether he had another point of view worthy of consideration, so that a choice could be made between the two opinions. Absalom's action was by God's ordering, because Ahithophel's plan was in fact sound and all the counselors approved it, but God allowed doubt in Absalom's heart, or he took care to add Hushai's counsel, perhaps so that the idea might be even more sound.

17.4.0.en: Hushai arrived and stood before Absalom, and Absalom set before him the plan Ahithophel had advised and asked him whether he supported it, so that it would be carried out, or whether he had another opinion, which he should present to him.

17.5.0.en: It was part of Hushai's wisdom that he acknowledged that Ahithophel's counsels had on many occasions been good and sound, because Ahithophel was one of the king's most important counselors, and he said this so that it would not be known from his opinion that he was prejudiced against Ahithophel, but he added that it was not good this time.

17.6.0.en: Hushai began to state the reasons for which he did not support Ahithophel's opinion. He mentioned that David's men were mighty men of war, and that they were in a state of great anger because of the events taking place, and that their anger was like the anger of a bear robbed of her cubs, which is seized by such fury that she devours everyone she meets. Moreover, David was a man of war with great knowledge and previous experience of its plans and the duties of precaution in them; he does not spend the night with his men, but chooses places that no one expects, such as digging a trench to spend the night in or hiding in one of the natural pits in case fighting breaks out between the two camps. And even if some of David's men were killed in the battle, counter-rumors could spread saying that those who were killed were Absalom's soldiers, and the morale of Absalom's army and of his followers among the people would be affected.

17.7.0.en: Even the brave and mighty soldiers of Absalom's army, though their hearts are strong as the heart of a lion, are struck to the core by rumors, and fear begins to spread in their hearts, because they know very well the courage of David and the heroes of his army and David's military abilities.

17.8.0.en: After Hushai had set out the reasons for his rejection of Ahithophel's plan, he began to give his own counsel, which was as follows:

17.8.1.en: All the tribes of Israel are to be summoned from the north of the land to the south, so that their number will be great, like the sand that is by the sea, and they will gather around Absalom to protect him on every side, and then attack David wherever he may be hiding, as the dew falls on the ground, and kill him and his men, so that not one of them is left alive.

17.9.0.en: Hushai goes on explaining his plan, setting out an imaginary picture that pleases Absalom's vanity. He says that if David in his flight takes refuge in some city, that city will be destroyed, as if its houses were tied with ropes and the ropes pulled, so that the houses fall and become heaps and ruins; he means that it will be easy to destroy because the army that is with Absalom is very large.

17.10.0.en: The good counsel of Ahithophel: that is, sound with respect to the killing of David, and the intended meaning is not that it was good in the eyes of God.

17.10.1.en: The imaginary picture that Hushai devised dazzled the minds of Absalom and his men, and displays of grandeur and pomp led them astray, as he imagined himself in the midst of tens of thousands of people surrounding him, striking down David and his followers and demolishing the cities in which they were hiding. Because he was proud, he accepted Hushai's counsel with great joy and was deceived by it, for pride blinds a man's eyes, and Absalom and his men decided that Hushai's plan was better than Ahithophel's plan. This was by God's ordering, for the sake of David's righteousness and Absalom's wickedness, and He persuaded Absalom and all the counselors of Hushai's plan in answer to David's prayer (ch. 15:31). Thus we see that with the temptation God makes the way of escape for His loving children: despite the danger of Ahithophel's counsel, God made Absalom accept Hushai's counsel and so saved their beloved David.

17.10.2.en: Man is often deceived by outward things and enticed by external appearances, so that he falls into pride and conceit and loses his goodness.

17.11.s.en: (3) Hushai informs the priests of the counsel

17.11.0.en: In fulfillment of David's instructions, Hushai conveyed to Zadok and Abiathar, the chief priests, the details of what had taken place in the session in which Absalom and his men consulted with his counselors.

17.12.0.en: As a precaution, lest Absalom turn to Ahithophel's plan and attack David that night, Hushai asked the two priests to advise David to cross the Jordan the same day to the east bank, so that he and his men would not perish before the attack of Absalom's army.

17.13.0.en: Ahimaaz and Jonathan: the sons of the priests Zadok and Abiathar (ch. 15:27). Ahimaaz and Jonathan were waiting by a well near Jerusalem called En-rogel, preferring not to stay inside the city, so that no one would suspect them when they left it to carry the news to David, and Zadok and Abiathar sent a maidservant to their sons carrying the news that had to be delivered to David.

17.14.0.en: Fine flour: choice flour from which various cakes are made.

17.14.1.en: Absalom also had spies in the area, and one of them discovered the movements of Ahimaaz and Jonathan and the maidservant and informed Absalom. Ahimaaz and Jonathan sensed that someone was watching them and expected Absalom to seize them, so they entered the house of a man in the village of Bahurim near Jerusalem, and his wife hid them in a dry well that was inside the house, and covered the well with a covering and spread fine flour on it, so that it would appear that the covering was spread on the ground with the flour on it and there was no well in the place.

17.14.2.en: We note that at the village of Bahurim Shimei stood gloating over David and cursing him, and in the same village God arranged the rescue of David's helpers, through this woman who loved David. So when we accept insults, God gives us deliverance for the sake of our humility.

17.15.0.en: What Ahimaaz and Jonathan had expected indeed happened, for some of Absalom's men came searching for them, as some of the inhabitants of the area had pointed them to the house they had entered. When the messengers asked the woman about them, she denied that they were in the house and claimed that they had crossed a brook near the house, so the messengers searched for them in the place and around it, and when they did not find them, they returned to Absalom. This was of course a lie, but God did not expose her, in order to save His good priests.

17.16.0.en: After the place was emptied of Absalom's messengers, Ahimaaz and Jonathan came out of the well in which they had been hidden and went at once to David and conveyed to him the message that came from Hushai the Archite and his advice that he cross the Jordan immediately, because Ahithophel had advised Absalom to attack him, but Hushai had postponed the attack for a few days so that he could prepare.

17.17.0.en: David acted on Hushai's advice, lest Absalom turn back and follow Ahithophel's words and attack him, so he and his men crossed to the east of the Jordan, and their crossing lasted all night, so that by the time daylight broke all had crossed. That is, all the events mentioned in this chapter took place in one day, ending with this night in which David crossed the Jordan River, which was very wearying for David and those with him.

17.17.1.en: The priests' sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan bore the risk to their lives in order to save David and those with him. So be courageous and help the needy and the wronged, even if you sacrifice some effort or money or anything you can offer, for you offer it to God in the person of these needy ones.

17.18.0.en: Ahithophel saw that his counsel had not been followed, and expected that Hushai's plan would lead to David's victory, so that he would return to his kingdom and take vengeance on him for his betrayal in joining Absalom. So he saddled his donkey and returned to his town, set his house in order, and then killed himself by hanging, and they buried him in the tomb of his father. Ahithophel here is a type of Judas Iscariot: after trying to kill David, who is a type of Christ, and failing, and feeling his sin, he despaired and killed himself.

17.18.1.en: Suicide is a great sin, for it means loss of hope and failure to surrender to God in all circumstances, so we must not lose confidence in His promises, but cling to them and never despair of His mercy. Whatever our faults, we repent and ask for His help, and He will save us and forgive our sins.

17.19.0.en: Mahanaim: it lies east of the Jordan and north of the Jabbok River, one of the tributaries of the Jordan, and it is fortified, so it suited David as a place to hide in.

17.19.1.en: After David crossed the Jordan, he reached Mahanaim, and Absalom acted on Hushai's counsel, gathering a huge army from all the tribes of Israel, and he also crossed the Jordan in preparation to meet the army of David his father.

17.20.0.en: Amasa: he is the son of Abigail, David's sister, so he is considered the cousin of Joab, the commander of David's army; he was an Ishmaelite on his father's side and an Israelite on his mother's side, and later Joab stabbed him treacherously with his sword. Abigail the daughter of Nahash: a half-sister of David.

17.20.1.en: Ithra the Israelite: an Ishmaelite man who married Abigail, David's sister, and was called the Israelite (1 Chr 2:17) because he joined the Jews.

17.20.2.en: Nahash: probably the king of the children of Ammon, who married a woman and then divorced her, and Jesse, David's father, married her and had two daughters by her, Zeruiah and Abigail, so they are David's sisters but only on the father's side.

17.20.3.en: Absalom appointed a man named Amasa as commander of his army, because Joab remained loyal to David. This Amasa was a son of Ithra.

17.21.0.en: Gilead: a large region lying east of the Jordan.

17.21.1.en: Absalom encamped with his great army in the hill country of Gilead, near the place where David had encamped, in preparation for attacking him.

17.22.0.en: Shobi the son of Nahash: an Ammonite man from Rabbah, the capital of the children of Ammon, who brought food for David and the people who were with him.

17.22.1.en: Machir the son of Ammiel: a man famous for doing good, who hosted in his house Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan until David summoned him to Jerusalem (ch. 9:3, 4). Lo-debar: a place in Gilead, now "Umm ed-Diyar," south of Wadi el-Arab east of the Jordan. Barzillai the Gileadite: a Gileadite man who was a friend of David and treated him well during his flight from Absalom, so David showed kindness to his family and charged Solomon his son to show kindness to the sons of Barzillai. Rogelim: a city in the land of Gilead, whose site today is Wadi er-Rujayla near Irbid. Beds: rugs and mats to lie on.

17.22.2.en: Basins: vessels in which food is placed.

17.22.3.en: Men loyal to David came to him at Mahanaim and brought him gifts, moved by love for him, loyalty to him, and compassion for their brothers who were with him. The men who came to him were Shobi the son of Nahash, Machir the son of Ammiel, and Barzillai the Gileadite.

17.22.4.en: The gifts they brought were as follows: beds to sit on, basins for putting water in for washing or for putting food in, and earthen vessels for cooking food.

17.22.5.en: Foodstuffs: wheat and barley, flour and parched corn; pulses: beans, lentils, and parched pulse; honey and butter, sheep for slaughter, and cheese of kine.

17.22.6.en: These loyal men appreciated the difficult circumstances surrounding the flight of David and his followers from Jerusalem, for they had left in haste and had not taken with them the means of living they needed, and had left behind everything they owned, walking long distances in the wilderness. They saw that the people were weary and hungry and thirsty, and they did not hesitate to supply them with what they saw they needed.

17.22.7.en: Some commentators hold that David sang Psalms 4 and 23 at this time, because they carry the meanings of trust in God and enjoyment of His care.

17.22.8.en: Great is God in His arrangements: He did not abandon David and those with him because they were wronged, but provided for all their material needs. So do not worry if you face problems or fear things that will happen in the future, because your God is responsible for you as long as you hold fast to Him, and He will never leave you.
